The Y chromosome plays a central role in male sex determination in humans through the SRY gene, which triggers testes development [d11][d5][d8][d14]. Specifically, the SRY gene on the Y chromosome overrides the biological default of female development and causes the male reproductive system to form [d11][d8]. However, the Y chromosome does not exclusively determine male gender: in Swyer syndrome, individuals with a 46,XY karyotype develop female reproductive structures and typically a female gender identity [d1], and in 46,XX testicular difference of sex development, a fetus without a Y chromosome can develop as male if the SRY gene is translocated onto an X chromosome [d12]. Beyond humans, sex determination is even more varied: in many reptiles, sex is determined by environmental temperature rather than chromosomes [d3][d6][d14], and other systems such as ZW (birds) and XO (insects) show that the Y chromosome is just one of many sex-determining mechanisms across species [d6]. Thus, while the Y chromosome is the primary driver of male sex development in typical human biology, genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors can all influence the outcome [d2][d4][d8].
